questions.stem: About what proportion of all the water on Earth is fresh water?
options: About 70%
About 3%
About 30%
About 50%
questions.explanation: About 97% of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans. Only about 3% is fresh, and most of that is not readily available for use.

questions.stem: Where is most of Earth's fresh water stored?
options: As water vapour in the atmosphere
As moisture held in the soil
In ice sheets and glaciers
In rivers and freshwater lakes
questions.explanation: Roughly two-thirds of fresh water is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers, and most of the rest is groundwater. Rivers, lakes, soil moisture and the atmosphere hold only a tiny fraction.

questions.stem: Why does the small amount of accessible fresh water lead communities to invest in dams and desalination plants?
options: Fresh water is unlimited, so dams and desalination plants are built mainly for recreation
Fresh water cannot be recycled, so every litre used is permanently lost from the water cycle
Fresh water occurs only in the oceans, so all drinking water must be made from seawater
Accessible surface water and groundwater are limited and variable, so supply must be secured
questions.explanation: Most fresh water is locked in ice or deep underground, and rainfall varies. Recognising this, communities invest in infrastructure that stores water or makes new supplies, such as dams and desalination plants.

questions.stem: Rainfall in south-west Western Australia has declined since the 1970s, but streamflow into Perth's dams has fallen by a much larger proportion. What best explains this?
options: Drier soils soak up more of each rainfall, so a small drop in rain causes a large drop in runoff
Less rain falls on the dams themselves, which accounts for most of the water they receive
Streamflow depends only on temperature, so warming alone has reduced the water reaching the dams
Desalination plants have taken water from the rivers that once flowed into the dams
questions.explanation: Runoff is what remains after the soil and vegetation have taken up water. When catchments are drier, more of each rainfall is absorbed, so runoff falls by a larger percentage than rainfall does.

questions.stem: How does reverse osmosis desalination produce fresh water?
options: Seawater is forced at high pressure through a membrane that holds back the salt
Seawater is boiled with solar energy and the salt is collected as it floats to the top
Seawater is mixed with fresh river water until the salt is diluted to safe levels
Seawater is frozen and the salt crystals are filtered out as the ice is melted again
questions.explanation: A semi-permeable membrane lets water molecules through but not dissolved salts. High pressure is needed to push water through it, which is why reverse osmosis uses a lot of energy.

questions.stem: What are the two main environmental concerns of seawater desalination plants?
options: Release of nutrients that cause algal blooms in nearby rivers and lakes
Clearing of large catchments and the loss of the forests within them
High energy use and the discharge of concentrated brine into the sea
Lowering of the water table and drying of nearby wetlands and lakes
questions.explanation: Reverse osmosis needs large amounts of electricity, which can mean greenhouse gas emissions unless renewable energy is used. It also returns a saltier, denser brine to the sea.

questions.stem: Why is brine from a desalination plant released through diffusers spread along the sea floor?
options: Brine is denser than seawater and could pool on the bottom, harming organisms that live there
Brine is less dense than seawater and would float, blocking sunlight from reaching the seagrass below
Brine is fresher than seawater and would lower the salinity of the whole coastal ocean
Brine is hotter than boiling water and must be cooled quickly so it does not scald fish
questions.explanation: Concentrated brine is denser than the surrounding seawater, so it tends to sink and spread along the bottom, where it can lower oxygen levels and stress benthic organisms. Diffusers mix it quickly so salinity stays near normal.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of desalination as a water source for a city in a drying climate?
options: It recharges coastal aquifers directly, so the water table rises around the plant
Its output does not depend on rainfall, so supply is secure during droughts
It uses less energy than any other water source, so it has no greenhouse emissions
It increases rainfall over the city by adding water vapour to the atmosphere
questions.explanation: A desalination plant draws on the ocean, so its output is independent of the rainfall that fills dams and recharges aquifers. Its main costs are energy and brine disposal.

questions.stem: A city in a drying climate must choose between a new dam on a river and a new desalination plant. Which argument best supports the desalination plant?
options: The plant would cost nothing to run, because seawater is free and needs no treatment
Inflows to a new dam would fall as rainfall declines, but the plant's output would not
The plant would use less energy than a dam, which needs large pumps to move all of its water
The plant would raise local rainfall, refilling the existing dams more quickly
questions.explanation: In a drying climate, a dam's yield depends on falling streamflow, while desalination is independent of rainfall. Desalination does use much more energy than gravity-fed dam supply, so energy is a cost to weigh, not an advantage.

questions.stem: What is aquifer recharge?
options: Water that soaks down to the water table and adds to the groundwater stored in an aquifer
Water that is pumped from an aquifer and used to irrigate crops on the land above it
Water that flows across the surface into rivers without soaking into the ground at all
Water that evaporates from the soil surface back into the atmosphere after rain falls
questions.explanation: Recharge is the inflow to groundwater, mainly rainfall that infiltrates through the soil. Sustainable groundwater use depends on keeping extraction within recharge.

questions.stem: Why do confined aquifers usually recharge much more slowly than shallow unconfined aquifers?
options: They are filled with seawater, so fresh rainfall cannot displace the water they already hold
They are capped by impermeable layers, so water enters only where the aquifer reaches the surface
They lie close to the surface, so most of the rain that reaches them evaporates before it can soak in
They contain no pore spaces, so water cannot move through them once it reaches the aquifer
questions.explanation: An impermeable confining layer stops rain soaking straight down, so a confined aquifer is recharged only in its outcrop area, which may be far away. Water then moves slowly through the rock, sometimes over thousands of years.

questions.stem: Pine plantations once covered large areas over the Gnangara groundwater system north of Perth. Why did harvesting them without replanting help aquifer recharge?
options: The pines intercepted rain and transpired water, so less reached the water table
The pines added salt to the soil, so their removal made the groundwater fresher
The pines' roots sealed the sandy soil, so no rain at all could soak downwards
The pines produced extra rainfall, so removing them reduced flooding of the aquifer
questions.explanation: Dense plantations catch rain on their canopy, where it evaporates, and draw soil water up through transpiration. Replacing them with lower vegetation lets more rainfall reach the groundwater.

questions.stem: Perth treats some wastewater to drinking-water standard and injects it into deep aquifers. How does this help the water supply?
options: It adds recharge that replaces water extracted from the aquifers, independent of rainfall
It removes all salt from the aquifers, turning brackish groundwater into fresh water
It raises the water table so high that wetlands flood and supply drinking water directly
It prevents any further extraction from the aquifers, so their storage cannot decline
questions.explanation: This is managed aquifer recharge. Recycled water tops up the aquifer so more groundwater can be drawn later, and it does not rely on rainfall.

questions.stem: A catchment of clay soils is covered by roads, roofs and car parks as a city grows. What is the most likely effect on local water resources?
options: More rain infiltrates through the hard surfaces, raising the water table across the city
Rainfall over the city stops, because hard surfaces do not release any water vapour
Runoff decreases, because hard surfaces store rainfall until it evaporates slowly
Less rain infiltrates and more runs off quickly, reducing recharge and increasing flooding
questions.explanation: Impervious surfaces stop water soaking in, so stormwater runs off rapidly into drains and streams. Less water reaches the aquifer unless the stormwater is directed to infiltration basins.

questions.stem: Groundwater is over-extracted when:
options: water is pumped out at night instead of during the day
recharge exceeds the volume of water that is pumped out
more water is pumped out than is replaced by recharge
water is pumped out at any rate from a confined aquifer
questions.explanation: Over-extraction means withdrawal exceeds recharge, so groundwater storage and the water table decline year after year.

questions.stem: Heavy pumping from bores near the coast lowers the water table in a coastal aquifer. What is a likely consequence?
options: Rainfall over the coast increases to replace the water pumped out
The aquifer fills with fresh water drawn in from the ocean floor
Seawater moves inland into the aquifer, making the bores salty
Fresh groundwater rises above the land surface and floods homes
questions.explanation: Fresh groundwater normally pushes against seawater beneath the coast. Lowering the fresh water level lets the denser seawater wedge move inland, and once bores turn saline they may be unusable for many years.

questions.stem: Why do some wetlands on the Swan Coastal Plain shrink or dry out when nearby groundwater pumping increases?
options: Their water is an exposed part of the water table, so they fall when it falls
Pumping adds salt to the wetlands, which evaporates them more quickly in summer
Pumping raises the water table, which drains the wetlands into nearby rivers
Their water comes only from rain, so pumping has no effect and they dry naturally
questions.explanation: Many coastal plain wetlands are windows onto the shallow water table. They are groundwater-dependent ecosystems, so a lower water table means lower wetland levels and stressed vegetation and fauna.

questions.stem: When a wetland's water table falls, iron sulfide-rich sediments that were waterlogged become exposed to air. Water quality then declines sharply. Why?
options: The sulfides dissolve in fresh water, which raises pH and makes the water alkaline
The sediments release extra oxygen, which kills the bacteria that clean the water
The sediments absorb all nutrients, so the algae that make oxygen cannot survive
The sulfides oxidise to sulfuric acid, which lowers pH and releases toxic metals
questions.explanation: These are acid sulfate soils. They are harmless while waterlogged, but exposure to oxygen produces sulfuric acid, which can mobilise metals such as aluminium and arsenic into the water.

questions.stem: Water authorities set aside environmental flows in regulated rivers. What is their main purpose?
options: To keep enough flow to sustain fish breeding, wetlands and other river ecosystems
To provide extra water for irrigation and town supply during the driest months of each year
To flush desalination brine out of the river mouth and back into the open sea
To lower river levels so that farmland beside the river never floods again
questions.explanation: Extraction for towns and farms reduces river flows. Environmental flows reserve part of the water so river and floodplain ecosystems that depend on natural flow patterns can persist.

questions.stem: A bore record shows the water table rising each winter and falling each summer, but the overall level has dropped by about 0.5 m per year for 20 years. Rainfall over that time has been steady. What is the best conclusion?
options: The bore has been measured with a faulty instrument
Extraction from the aquifer is exceeding its recharge
Recharge is exceeding extraction from the aquifer
The seasonal changes show the aquifer is in balance
questions.explanation: The seasonal cycle reflects winter recharge and summer use, but the long-term downward trend with steady rainfall means more water is leaving than entering. A single faulty instrument would not give a steady trend over two decades.

questions.stem: In the Western Australian Wheatbelt, dryland salinity was caused mainly by:
options: planting too many deep-rooted trees, which pulled salt up from deep in the rock
clearing deep-rooted native vegetation and replacing it with shallow-rooted annual crops
irrigating crops with seawater pumped inland from the coast through long pipelines
salt carried inland by cyclones and dropped directly onto paddocks by heavy rain
questions.explanation: Native woodland used nearly all the rainfall. Annual crops and pastures use much less, so more water reaches the groundwater and the water table rises, bringing stored salt with it.

questions.stem: Why does a rising water table cause salt to appear at the soil surface?
options: Groundwater is always seawater, so any rise brings ocean salt directly to the surface of the paddock
Rising groundwater pushes salt crystals up through the soil like a piston from below
Groundwater reacts with the soil to form salt as it rises towards the root zone
Groundwater dissolves stored salt, then evaporates near the surface and leaves it behind
questions.explanation: Salt stored in the soil profile dissolves in the rising groundwater. Once the water table is within a couple of metres of the surface, water is drawn up and evaporates, concentrating the salt where plant roots grow.

questions.stem: After much of a river's catchment was cleared for farming, the river water became too salty to drink. Which process caused this?
options: Rising saline groundwater seeped into the streams that feed the river
Farm fertiliser reacted with the river water to form dissolved salts
Cleared land produced less runoff, so rain no longer reached the river
Livestock drank fresh water from the river, leaving only salty water
questions.explanation: Clearing raised water tables across the catchment, and saline groundwater discharged into creeks and rivers. Land clearing therefore affects both land and the quality of surface water.

questions.stem: Which action would best reduce rising saline water tables in a cleared catchment?
options: Spreading extra irrigation water to wash the salt down below the root zone each year
Building more impervious surfaces so that rain cannot soak into the ground at all
Planting deep-rooted perennial trees and shrubs in the areas where recharge occurs
Clearing the remaining native vegetation so that more water can evaporate from soil
questions.explanation: Deep-rooted perennials use more water throughout the year, reducing recharge and lowering the water table. Extra irrigation adds water to the groundwater and makes the problem worse.

questions.stem: Native vegetation is cleared from steep slopes above a river. Over the next few years the river becomes more turbid after rain and its pools fill with silt. Which explanation fits best?
options: Without trees, rainfall over the slopes stops, so the river dries and pools fill with dust
Without vegetation, the soil becomes more permeable, so water no longer runs off the slopes
Without leaf litter, the river water becomes saltier, which makes particles settle quickly
Without roots and ground cover, rain erodes the soil and runoff carries it into the river
questions.explanation: Vegetation intercepts rain and roots bind soil. Clearing increases runoff and erosion, adding sediment that makes water turbid, smothers habitats and fills pools.

questions.stem: Which two nutrients are mainly responsible for eutrophication of waterways?
options: Iron and aluminium
Nitrogen and phosphorus
Sodium and chlorine
Oxygen and hydrogen
questions.explanation: Nitrogen and phosphorus usually limit the growth of algae and aquatic plants, so adding them causes blooms. Sodium and chloride are the ions of salt, which cause salinity rather than eutrophication.

questions.stem: Eutrophication of a waterway is:
options: enrichment with nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, causing excess algal growth
enrichment with dissolved oxygen, causing fish populations to grow out of control
the gradual increase in salt levels after a catchment is cleared for farming
the gradual filling of a lake with sediment eroded from its surrounding catchment
questions.explanation: Excess nutrients fuel rapid growth of algae and aquatic plants. The consequences include low oxygen, loss of other species and sometimes toxic blooms.

questions.stem: Fertiliser washes into a lake. Which sequence of events most likely follows?
options: Bacteria decompose fertiliser, oxygen rises, algae die, fish numbers grow
Fish eat the fertiliser, fish numbers grow, algae are eaten, water clears
Algae die at once, oxygen rises, bacteria starve, fish numbers increase
Algal bloom, algae die, bacteria decompose them and use oxygen, fish die
questions.explanation: Nutrients cause an algal bloom. When the algae die, decomposing bacteria consume dissolved oxygen, and low oxygen can kill fish and other animals.

questions.stem: Which of these is a major source of the phosphorus that causes eutrophication in rivers draining farmland and suburbs?
options: Salt carried up by rising groundwater beneath the land
Carbon dioxide released by fish breathing in the river
Fertiliser washed or leached from paddocks and gardens
Oxygen dissolved from the air at the water surface
questions.explanation: Fertilisers, animal manure, sewage and some detergents add phosphorus and nitrogen to waterways. Salt causes salinity, not eutrophication.

questions.stem: Phosphorus fertiliser applied to farms on the deep sandy soils of the Swan Coastal Plain reaches rivers and estuaries more readily than fertiliser on clay-rich soils. Why?
options: Sandy soils are impermeable, so all fertiliser runs off the surface into the rivers
Sandy soils produce phosphorus naturally, which adds to the fertiliser applied
Sandy soils have little clay or organic matter to bind phosphorus, so it leaches easily
Sandy soils contain more clay than other soils, so they release stored phosphorus whenever they are wet
questions.explanation: Clay minerals and iron and aluminium oxides hold phosphorus, but these sands contain little of them. Rain washes phosphorus down through the sand into groundwater and drains that feed waterways.

questions.stem: Severe algal blooms in the Peel-Harvey estuary led to a channel being cut to connect it more directly with the ocean. How did the channel reduce the blooms?
options: Seawater killed every alga in the estuary at once, so no further blooms could occur
The channel drained the estuary completely, so no water remained for algae to grow
The channel added phosphorus from the ocean, which algae cannot use for growth
Increased tidal flushing carried nutrients and algae out to sea and diluted them
questions.explanation: Better exchange with the ocean diluted and removed nutrient-rich estuary water. It managed the symptoms, so reducing nutrient inputs from the catchment is still needed.

questions.stem: Some algal blooms are formed by cyanobacteria. Why do authorities close affected waterways to people and animals?
options: Cyanobacteria remove all salt from the water, so it can no longer be drunk
Cyanobacteria release radioactive gases when they float near the surface
Some cyanobacteria produce toxins harmful to people, pets and livestock
Cyanobacteria raise the water temperature to levels that burn the skin
questions.explanation: Toxins from blooms can cause skin irritation, illness and even livestock deaths, making the water unsafe for drinking, swimming or stock.

questions.stem: Downstream of a dairy farm, a creek has high nitrate and phosphate levels, low dissolved oxygen and recent fish kills. Which management would best address the cause?
options: Add more fertiliser upstream so that algae there use up the extra nutrients
Remove all trees along the creek so more sunlight can reach the water surface
Pump the creek dry each summer so that algae have no water left to grow in
Fence cattle out of the creek, plant riparian buffers and reduce fertiliser use
questions.explanation: Reducing nutrient inputs tackles the cause. Riparian vegetation traps nutrients and sediment in runoff, and fencing keeps manure out of the water. More sunlight would encourage algal growth.

questions.stem: The concept of an ecological footprint is used to measure:
options: the volume of fresh water a population uses each year for drinking only
the productive land and water area needed to supply a population and absorb its wastes
the area of land that a population's houses, roads and other buildings physically cover
the number of species a population has driven to extinction in its region
questions.explanation: An ecological footprint converts the demand of producing, harvesting, transporting and processing resources, and assimilating the wastes, into an equivalent area of biologically productive land and water.

questions.stem: In what unit is an ecological footprint usually expressed?
options: Megalitres of water
Kilojoules of energy
Global hectares
Tonnes of carbon
questions.explanation: Footprints are expressed in global hectares, hectares with world-average biological productivity, so that different land and sea types can be added together and compared.

questions.stem: For high-income countries, the largest part of the ecological footprint is usually the area needed to:
options: grow the cotton and wool used to make clothing each year
provide space for houses, roads and other infrastructure
supply fresh water for drinking and household purposes
absorb the carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels
questions.explanation: The carbon component, the forest area needed to absorb carbon dioxide emissions, dominates the footprint of most high-income countries. Reducing fossil fuel use therefore reduces the footprint most.

questions.stem: Humanity's total ecological footprint is larger than Earth's biocapacity. What does this mean?
options: The footprint is measured wrongly, because demand can never exceed biocapacity
Every country uses less than its own share, so there is no global shortage of resources
Resources are used faster than they regenerate, and wastes such as carbon dioxide build up
Earth produces more resources each year than people can possibly use, so stocks build up steadily
questions.explanation: This is overshoot: demand exceeds what ecosystems can regenerate in a year. It is possible only by running down stocks, such as fish and forests, and letting wastes accumulate.

questions.stem: The average footprint in a country is 6 global hectares per person. Earth's biocapacity is about 1.5 global hectares per person. How many Earths would be needed if everyone lived this way?
questions.explanation: Earths needed = footprint per person ÷ biocapacity per person = 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4. Multiplying the two numbers gives 9, and dividing the other way gives 0.25.

questions.stem: A town of 20 000 people has an average footprint of 7 global hectares per person. The productive land and water around it provide 50 000 global hectares. Which statement is correct?
options: Its footprint is 2857 gha, so it uses only a small part of its own local biocapacity
Its footprint is 7 gha, so it is well within the 50 000 gha of local biocapacity
Its footprint is 140 000 gha, so it relies on resources and waste absorption from elsewhere
Its footprint is 140 000 gha, so it has a surplus of 90 000 gha to supply to other regions nearby
questions.explanation: Total footprint = 20 000 × 7 = 140 000 gha, which exceeds local biocapacity by 90 000 gha. That deficit is met by imports and by emissions absorbed, or not absorbed, elsewhere.

questions.stem: Why does the ecological footprint of food imported from overseas include the fuel used to ship it?
options: Transporting resources uses energy and produces carbon dioxide that must be absorbed
Shipping adds nutrients to the food, which increases the cropland it represents
Imported food is counted twice, once in each country, to make footprints larger
Fuel is a renewable resource, so it is added to the footprint as productive land
questions.explanation: A footprint includes producing, harvesting, transporting and processing resources and assimilating the wastes. Fuel burnt in transport adds to the carbon component.
